questions.q: What is true about pod-to-pod network access in a default Kubernetes cluster, with no NetworkPolicy resources created?
options: Only Pods in the same namespace can reach each other
Every Pod can reach every other Pod, with no restrictions at all, regardless of namespace
Pods can only reach each other through an Ingress controller
All Pod traffic is denied until a NetworkPolicy explicitly allows it
questions.explain: By default, a stock Kubernetes cluster applies zero network restrictions between Pods — any Pod can open a connection to any other Pod, in any namespace, until a NetworkPolicy says otherwise.

questions.q: What does podSelector at the top level of a NetworkPolicy's spec determine?
options: Which container image the policy applies to
Which Pods the policy itself applies to — the Pods being protected by its rules
Which namespace the NetworkPolicy resource is stored in
Which Ingress controller enforces the policy
questions.explain: podSelector picks the set of Pods this policy governs. An empty podSelector: {} selects every Pod in the namespace.

questions.q: In the allow-frontend-to-api example, which Pods are permitted to connect to payments-api after the policy is applied?
options: Only Pods labeled app: frontend, and only over TCP port 8080
Any Pod in the billing namespace, on any port
Any Pod in the cluster, as long as it uses TCP
No Pods at all — the policy blocks every connection
questions.explain: The ingress rule's from.podSelector restricts allowed sources to Pods labeled app: frontend, and the ports list restricts it further to TCP port 8080 — everything else is denied once the policy exists.

questions.q: Why does a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy use podSelector: {} with no ingress or egress rules listed?
options: podSelector: {} only applies to Pods without any labels at all
This configuration is invalid and Kubernetes rejects it
It makes the policy apply only to the kube-system namespace
An empty podSelector selects every Pod in the namespace, and listing no rules blocks all traffic for those Pods by default
questions.explain: podSelector: {} matches every Pod in the namespace it's created in. With policyTypes set but no ingress/egress entries, every matched Pod has all that traffic denied, which is the standard safe starting point before adding narrow allow-rules.

questions.q: Why might creating a NetworkPolicy resource have no actual effect on traffic in some clusters?
options: NetworkPolicy resources only take effect inside the default namespace
NetworkPolicy only governs traffic to Services, never to Pods directly
NetworkPolicy rules only take effect if the cluster's installed CNI plugin actually enforces them — some basic CNI setups ignore them entirely
NetworkPolicy resources expire automatically after 24 hours unless renewed
questions.explain: A NetworkPolicy is a declarative resource; enforcing it is the CNI plugin's job. Plugins like Calico or Cilium enforce it, but some simpler CNI setups silently ignore NetworkPolicy objects altogether.
